system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2137-12-06 20:17:00 to 2137-12-07 15:27:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for progressive dyspnea and increased sputum production in the setting of tracheostomy and recurrent tracheobronchial stenosis. He was found to have tracheobronchitis due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa, confirmed by sputum and bronchial cultures. He was treated with IV cefepime, later transitioned to oral ciprofloxacin, and received two bronchoscopies with balloon dilation of the trachea and left main bronchus. His prednisone dose was increased to 20 mg daily to reduce airway inflammation and then tapered. A new humidifier was arranged due to risk of equipment contamination. He improved clinically, maintained oxygenation on room air, and was discharged home with follow-up planned in pulmonary and infectious disease clinics.
problems: Other specified congenital malformation syndromes, not elsewhere classified
Pseudomonas (aeruginosa) (mallei) (pseudomallei) as the cause of diseases classified elsewhere

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospital doctors. You've just come up from the procedure suite after your bronchoscopy and dilation. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, doctor. I’m okay. My throat hurts, maybe a 6 out of 10. But it’s better since I got the pain medicine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. The bronchoscopy can cause some irritation and soreness. We’ll keep the oxycodone available for you as needed. You’re breathing well, and your trach is stable. Any chest pain or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just the throat pain. No shortness of breath. I feel pretty comfortable sitting up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We did a balloon dilation to open up some narrow areas in your airway, which is part of your ongoing care for the tracheal stenosis. We also cleaned out some secretions and removed a small pseudomembrane. Biopsies were taken to check for inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was anything abnormal in the biopsy? Or the washings?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The initial report shows inflammation and granulation tissue, which is expected. No signs of infection or cancer. The bronchial wash showed lots of white blood cells, which means there’s inflammation, but no organisms were seen on the gram stain yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time we found Pseudomonas. Could it be back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The culture is still growing. There’s a gram-negative rod, but we won’t know exactly what it is for a few days. If it’s an infection, we’ll adjust treatment, but right now you’re not showing signs of active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. Your vitals are stable, you’re not spiking a fever, and your breathing is good. The main issue right now is post-procedure pain, which we’re managing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the steroids? Last time I was on a higher dose after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. We’re starting you on prednisone 50 mg daily for five days to reduce airway inflammation from the procedure. Then you’ll go back to your usual 7.5 mg daily after that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my other meds—methotrexate, famotidine—should I keep those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue all your home medications. We’ve listed them in your chart. Methotrexate for your relapsing polychondritis, famotidine for reflux, and your calcium and vitamin D.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did well overnight. Your breathing stayed stable, and the chest X-ray shows no complications like a pneumothorax. The trach tube is in a good position.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if everything stays the same. We’ll discharge you later this morning. You’ll need to follow up with Dr. ___ in interventional pulmonology in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start feeling worse—like more pain or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back if you develop fever, chills, increased secretions, or worsening shortness of breath. Otherwise, keep taking the prednisone as prescribed and rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready, including a small supply of oxycodone for breakthrough pain. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it, doctor. Feels good to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ve tolerated the procedure well and recovered quickly. Just keep an eye on how you feel over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. And I’ll call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Your rheumatology team also knows about this admission, so no changes to your methotrexate. Stay hydrated and keep using your humidifier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I always do. That humidifier’s been a lifesaver since last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. We’ll have the nurse go over your discharge instructions one more time before you leave. Take it easy, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for post-procedural monitoring after undergoing a flexible bronchoscopy with balloon dilation for recurrent tracheal stenosis related to relapsing polychondritis. He experienced throat pain post-procedure, which was managed with oxycodone. He remained stable throughout the admission with no respiratory compromise. A short course of prednisone was initiated to reduce airway inflammation. Bronchial washings showed gram-negative rods pending culture, but no acute infection was evident. He was discharged home the following morning with instructions to follow up in interventional pulmonology and to complete the steroid taper.
